description: The DOSTEL detector measured radiation inside Europe's Columbus lab on the ISS. Astronauts receive about as much radiation in one day up there as you get in a whole year on Earth!
An upgraded version of DOSTEL kept tracking radiation levels. During solar storms, the dose rate can jump up even higher — that's when astronauts need extra shielding!
The Bulgarian-made Liulin detector helped scientists track radiation in the Russian part of the station. Different spots on the ISS get slightly different radiation levels!
NASA's own radiation detector has been monitoring dose rates since the early days of the ISS. It helps keep astronauts safe by tracking how much radiation they receive.
During the famous Halloween Solar Storms of 2003, radiation levels spiked way above normal! The crew took shelter in the most shielded parts of the station.
During solar minimum (when the Sun is quiet), cosmic rays from deep space actually increase! Without the Sun's magnetic field pushing them away, more sneak through.
The Tissue Equivalent Proportional Counter mimics how human tissue absorbs radiation. It helps scientists figure out how much radiation an astronaut's body actually receives.
The Zvezda module is one of the oldest parts of the ISS. Its walls provide some shielding, but cosmic rays still get through — they can even pass through your hand!
The X9.3 solar flare in September 2017 pushed radiation levels higher than usual on the ISS. Luckily, Earth's magnetic field helped protect the station.
Solar Cycle 24 was winding down, so radiation from the Sun was low. But galactic cosmic rays from exploding stars far away were at their highest!
The Radiation Environment Monitor tracks radiation in real time. When levels spike during a solar event, it helps Mission Control warn the crew to take shelter.
Japan's Kibo module has less shielding in some areas, so radiation readings can be a bit higher. Scientists use this data to design better shielding for future spacecraft.
